The Brown sicklebill (Epimachus meyeri) is a large paradisaeid endemic to the montane forests of New Guinea. Neonates, which emerge after an incubation period of approximately 21 days [ab = approximately 21 days] conducted at 34 °C [T = 34 °C], are remarkably altricial and weigh only 13.8 grams [Wwb = 13.8 grams] at hatching. This modest birth mass is consistent with a life-history strategy that prioritizes rapid postnatal development under extended parental care. The chick's initial body mass is substantially lower than the ultimate adult dimensions attained later in life, reflecting a pronounced ontogenetic growth trajectory. Interestingly, the incubation temperature of 34 °C [T = 34 °C] is notably lower than the deep-body temperature typical of active adult birds, a divergence that may influence the metabolic rate of the developing embryo.

Fledging, defined as the achievement of sustained flight and nest departure, occurs at 28 days after hatching [tx = 28 days after hatching] at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This relatively rapid attainment of flight capability is likely an adaptation to reduce nest predation risk in the dense montane understory. The age at fledging is followed later by the onset of gonadal maturation; puberty, or the attainment of full reproductive capacity, is reached at 84 days after hatching [tp = 84 days after hatching], a delay that reflects the substantial energetic investment required for the completion of skeletal and muscular growth before reproductive effort can be initiated at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C].

Significant sexual dimorphism in body size is a hallmark of this species, with adult males attaining a substantially greater asymptotic mass than females. This pronounced size disparity is reflected in differences in foraging ecology and social display behavior, and it likely contributes to the marked divergence in the species' overall life-history timing between the sexes. In comparative terms, the female asymptotic mass is modest relative to the male's, a pattern common among lek-breeding birds where male-male competition places a premium on large body size and energetic reserves.

Reproductive activity in the Brown sicklebill is characterized by a low annual output, consistent with its position as a large, long-lived forest bird. Available data indicate that females typically produce a single egg per clutch [N_R_i = single egg per clutch], and they raise only about one clutch per year [F_R_i = about one clutch per year]. This extremely low clutch size is one of the smallest recorded among passerines and represents a substantial energetic investment per offspring. The extended period of parental care, culminating in fledging at 28 days after hatching [tx = 28 days after hatching], necessitates a prolonged period of post-breeding recovery for the adult female at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. The first successful breeding event typically does not occur until an estimated 2.1 years since birth [tR = 2.1 years since birth], a delay that allows for the complete development of the ornate adult plumage and the learning of complex courtship displays at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C].
